notes: Twenty-two newly authored SSC-level writing prompts and illustrative answers: seven completing stories and fifteen dialogues. NOT recovered board/school questions, official exercises, exam predictions or official answer keys. There is no external source PDF, fabricated checksum, school or board attribution for these prompts.

Authored to close the numerical practice deficits in completing-story/dialogue categories, not original-exam stock deficits. Existing 33 story and 25 dialogue source exercises remain separate. Original-source quotas are not satisfied by these authored records.

Every story has a title, exact supplied beginning and ten separate continuation sentences. Every dialogue has twelve alternating turns between the named participants. These are possible responses, not exclusive canonical answers. Current practice blueprint assigns fifteen marks; there are no invented historical marks.

Deduplication is by scenario and communicative purpose, not only exact text. Science-fair error is distinct from found-money honesty; publishing-image permission from found property; bus journey planning from road-accident prevention; training-course evaluation from general unemployment; quiet wildlife observation from wetland community conservation. Related topics can share educational themes but are not counted as additional original exam sources.

General health/safety, safeguarding, privacy and disability content requires teacher review. No personalised treatment, chemical dose, installation/repair instruction, unsafe rescue or promise of guaranteed employment/harvest/energy output. Adult/qualified assistance used where appropriate. Fictional notices/events are not real-world alerts.

Authored status is always visible in each question instruction and draft name, even with provenance labels off. No boardSource/schoolSource, passage, sourceFile or invented literature attributed. Board-year filters must exclude this practice. Preview -> explicit consent -> Pending -> ADMIN review unchanged; no production import or approval.

items.learningFocus: Evidence, correction and scientific integrity; distinct from found-money honesty stories.
items.beginning: The school science fair was due to begin in an hour. Nabila checked her group’s water-saving model once more and noticed that the figures on their poster did not match the notebook. Her teammates wanted to leave the poster unchanged because the visitors were already arriving...
continuationSentences: Nabila asked the group to compare the measurements before presenting their work.
They discovered that one amount had been copied into the wrong column.
Their model still worked, but it saved less water than the poster claimed.
One teammate worried that correcting the figure would cost them a prize.
Nabila replied that the visitors deserved an honest explanation of the experiment.
The group agreed and neatly replaced the incorrect number.
When the judges arrived, they explained both their method and their mistake.
The judges asked useful questions and encouraged them to repeat the trial.
Although another team won first place, their teacher praised their careful correction.
The group left the fair determined to value reliable evidence more than an impressive claim.

items.learningFocus: Accessibility and shared decision-making; no unsafe lifting or pity-based resolution.
items.beginning: Our class had arranged an exhibition on the first floor of the school. Just before it opened, I learnt that our invited guest, a former student who used a wheelchair, could not reach the room. Everyone looked at the narrow staircase...
continuationSentences: I went to our teacher instead of trying to carry the guest up the stairs.
She asked the guest which arrangements would work best.
The guest suggested using an accessible room on the ground floor.
With permission, we moved the displays into the large room beside the entrance.
Some classmates cleared the doorway while others arranged wide spaces between the tables.
We checked the route with our guest and made further changes after listening to her.
She explored the exhibits independently and discussed her own school memories with us.
Other visitors also found the new arrangement easier to use.
Afterwards, we asked the school committee to consider accessibility when planning future events.
We understood that inclusion begins with listening and removing barriers, not making decisions for others.

items.learningFocus: Verification and responsible correction; no invented actual school announcement.
items.beginning: On Sunday evening, Sohan received a screenshot saying that Monday’s examination had been cancelled. Several classmates were already celebrating in their group chat. He was about to forward the picture when he noticed that the date at the top had been cut off...
continuationSentences: Sohan paused and asked where the screenshot had come from.
Nobody in the group could identify an official announcement.
He checked the school’s usual notice channel but found no cancellation.
With his parent’s help, he contacted the class teacher through the agreed school channel.
The teacher confirmed that the examination would take place as scheduled.
She explained that the screenshot showed an old notice from a different term.
Sohan shared the verified information without repeating anyone’s private contact details.
He also asked classmates who had forwarded the rumour to post a correction.
The next morning, the class arrived prepared instead of relying on the misleading picture.
They agreed to check the source and date of important messages before sharing them.

items.learningFocus: Maintenance reporting and water conservation; children do not attempt electrical or plumbing repairs.
items.beginning: Every afternoon, water collected beside the playground tap. Most students stepped around the puddle and hurried home. One day, Mariam saw that the tap was still running even though nobody was using it...
continuationSentences: Mariam noticed that the handle was broken and could not be closed normally.
She kept away from the slippery patch and told the school caretaker.
The caretaker put a warning beside the wet ground and informed the headteacher.
A qualified worker isolated the supply and replaced the damaged tap.
While waiting, the class used another approved drinking-water point.
Mariam and her friends suggested a simple way to report damaged school facilities.
Their teacher placed a maintenance notebook in the office.
Students began reporting broken lights, loose fittings and leaks to responsible adults.
The office checked the reports regularly instead of leaving them unanswered.
The small puddle had taught the class that noticing a problem should lead to responsible action.

items.learningFocus: Bystander support and reporting; no violent retaliation or instant guaranteed recovery.
items.beginning: A new student named Rafi joined our class halfway through the year. During group work, two classmates laughed at his accent and nobody offered him a place. I saw him close his notebook and move towards an empty desk...
continuationSentences: I invited Rafi to join our group and made room for his notebook.
When the laughter continued, I said calmly that his accent was not a reason to mock him.
Our teacher noticed the disturbance and spoke with the students involved.
She checked privately how Rafi wanted the situation handled.
In our project discussion, he suggested a useful way to organise the information.
We divided the work fairly and made sure everyone could contribute.
After class, one of the students apologised without making excuses.
The teacher reminded us how to report bullying and obtain support.
Rafi gradually became more comfortable, although we knew trust would take time.
We learnt that a welcoming classroom requires everyday respect rather than a single friendly gesture.

items.learningFocus: Cooperation and small-scale record-keeping; not a guaranteed agricultural outcome or seed-treatment guide.
items.beginning: After a difficult growing season, our neighbourhood gardening club had very few seeds for its small vegetable plots. Some members suggested abandoning the project. Then an elderly gardener opened a carefully labelled box...
continuationSentences: The box contained seeds she had saved from several suitable garden plants.
She explained that the names and collection dates helped her keep track of them.
The club asked a local agricultural adviser which seeds were appropriate for the coming season.
Together, they selected a small trial instead of promising a full harvest.
Members shared the available seeds fairly and recorded who planted each variety.
They prepared the plots with guidance and watered them carefully.
Not every seed germinated, so the group noted the failures as well as the successes.
At the next meeting, members compared their records and discussed what to change.
They agreed to save suitable seeds again and seek advice before expanding.
The project continued because people shared knowledge and effort rather than depending on a miracle.

tasks.answer:

After a difficult growing season, our neighbourhood gardening club had very few seeds for its small vegetable plots. Some members suggested abandoning the project. Then an elderly gardener opened a carefully labelled box...
The box contained seeds she had saved from several suitable garden plants. She explained that the names and collection dates helped her keep track of them. The club asked a local agricultural adviser which seeds were appropriate for the coming season. Together, they selected a small trial instead of promising a full harvest. Members shared the available seeds fairly and recorded who planted each variety. They prepared the plots with guidance and watered them carefully. Not every seed germinated, so the group noted the failures as well as the successes. At the next meeting, members compared their records and discussed what to change. They agreed to save suitable seeds again and seek advice before expanding. The project continued because people shared knowledge and effort rather than depending on a miracle.

items.learningFocus: Copyright, consent and attribution; credit alone is not represented as permission.
items.beginning: For our school magazine, I submitted a photograph of a craftsman working in the market. The editor liked it and asked me to write the caption. Only then did I remember that I had downloaded the picture from someone else’s page...
continuationSentences: I told the editor that I had not taken the photograph myself.
She paused the layout and asked me to identify its creator.
We found the photographer’s original page and checked the stated usage conditions.
There was no permission for us to republish the image.
With our teacher’s help, we sent a polite request instead of assuming that a credit line was enough.
When no reply arrived before the deadline, we chose not to use it.
I arranged to take a different photograph with an adult’s support and the subject’s informed agreement.
We checked the new caption and used the image only in the agreed school magazine.
The editor added a checklist for permissions and credits to our publication process.
I learnt that material being easy to download does not make it free to reuse.

tasks.instruction:
Authored practice — not a board or school examination question.
Topic: A borrowed photograph without permission
Read the beginning below. Write at least ten new sentences to complete the story and give it a suitable title.
For our school magazine, I submitted a photograph of a craftsman working in the market. The editor liked it and asked me to write the caption. Only then did I remember that I had downloaded the picture from someone else’s page...
tasks.answer:
The Photograph and the Credit
For our school magazine, I submitted a photograph of a craftsman working in the market. The editor liked it and asked me to write the caption. Only then did I remember that I had downloaded the picture from someone else’s page...
I told the editor that I had not taken the photograph myself. She paused the layout and asked me to identify its creator. We found the photographer’s original page and checked the stated usage conditions. There was no permission for us to republish the image. With our teacher’s help, we sent a polite request instead of assuming that a credit line was enough. When no reply arrived before the deadline, we chose not to use it. I arranged to take a different photograph with an adult’s support and the subject’s informed agreement. We checked the new caption and used the image only in the agreed school magazine. The editor added a checklist for permissions and credits to our publication process. I learnt that material being easy to download does not make it free to reuse.

items.learningFocus: Practical waste prevention and adult handling; no unsupported recycling guarantees.

tasks.instruction:
Authored practice — not a board or school examination question.
Topic: Separating school waste
Suppose you are Asha and your friend is Bithi. Write a dialogue about organising waste separation at school, including what to do when suitable collection services are unavailable.
tasks.answer:
Asha: Our classroom bin contains food scraps, paper and broken plastic together. Could we improve this?
Bithi: Yes, but we should first ask the school how the waste is collected after it leaves our room.
Asha: Otherwise, different bins might simply be emptied into the same container.
Bithi: Exactly. Let us speak with the caretaker and find out which materials the local collector accepts.
Asha: We could also reduce waste by bringing reusable lunch boxes and bottles.
Bithi: Clean paper might be collected separately if there is a reliable recycling service.
Asha: Should students sort through the existing mixed rubbish?
Bithi: No. We should not handle sharp, dirty or unknown materials. Responsible adults should manage those safely.
Asha: What if separate collection is not available yet?
Bithi: Then we can focus on reducing waste and ask the school to explore suitable arrangements.
Asha: We should use clear labels only after the collection plan is agreed.
Bithi: Good idea. A useful system needs follow-through, not just colourful bins.

items.learningFocus: General hygiene literacy; no chemical dosage or claim that appearance proves safety.

tasks.instruction:
Authored practice — not a board or school examination question.
Topic: Protecting drinking water at school
Suppose you are Rina and your friend is Tania. Write a dialogue about responding responsibly when students are concerned about the school drinking-water supply.
tasks.answer:
Rina: Some students are worried about the water point near our classroom. What should we do?
Tania: We should report the concern to a teacher rather than spread an unverified claim that it is unsafe.
Rina: The storage container looks dirty. Can appearance tell us whether the water is safe?
Tania: Not reliably. Clear water can also contain harmful contamination, so responsible testing and maintenance matter.
Rina: Should we pour a cleaning chemical into the tank ourselves?
Tania: Certainly not. Only trained, responsible people should manage cleaning and any treatment.
Rina: Meanwhile, we can ask the school which drinking-water point has been approved for use.
Tania: Yes, and bring water from a reliable source in a clean, covered container when possible.
Rina: We should avoid touching the inside of shared containers or leaving taps open.
Tania: The school also needs a regular cleaning and checking schedule.
Rina: I will explain our observations to the class teacher today.
Tania: Let us ask for clear guidance so everyone can follow the same safe arrangements.

items.learningFocus: Source/date checks, corrections and privacy; no fictional claim presented as an actual alert.

tasks.instruction:
Authored practice — not a board or school examination question.
Topic: Checking a viral online claim
Suppose you are Sami and your friend is Nila. Write a dialogue about checking a surprising online claim before sharing it.
tasks.answer:
Sami: This post says our town will have no electricity for a whole week. Shall I forward it?
Nila: First, check who published it and whether it has a date and a link to an official notice.
Sami: It is a screenshot with no source. Many people have shared it, though.
Nila: Popularity does not prove accuracy. It could be old, altered or taken out of context.
Sami: Where should we look for confirmation?
Nila: We can check the relevant service provider’s usual announcements and reliable reporting.
Sami: What if we cannot confirm it?
Nila: We should not present it as fact. We can ask a trusted adult to help us verify it.
Sami: I already sent it to two classmates. That was careless.
Nila: Send a correction explaining that it is unverified, without embarrassing anyone who believed it.
Sami: I will also avoid opening the strange sign-up link below the post.
Nila: Sensible. Checking the source protects both our information and our privacy.

items.learningFocus: Multiple access needs, privacy and autonomy; not pity or unsolicited physical assistance.

tasks.instruction:
Authored practice — not a board or school examination question.
Topic: Making a school event accessible
Suppose you are Mitu and your friend is Farhan. Write a dialogue about making a school event accessible to participants with different disabilities.
tasks.answer:
Mitu: We are planning the annual exhibition. How can we make it more accessible?
Farhan: We should ask participants about their access needs instead of guessing what they can do.
Mitu: A ground-floor venue and clear routes could help people with mobility needs.
Farhan: Yes, and the school should check entrances, seating and accessible facilities with the people concerned.
Mitu: What about information during the presentations?
Farhan: Clear written instructions, readable signs and captions where available can help more people participate.
Mitu: Should we automatically take someone’s arm to guide them?
Farhan: No. Ask whether they want assistance and how they prefer it to be offered.
Mitu: We also need a way to request arrangements privately.
Farhan: Our teacher can coordinate that without publicly sharing anyone’s personal information.
Mitu: Let us include accessibility in the first plan, not as a last-minute favour.
Farhan: Agreed. Participation should not depend on overcoming barriers that we could remove.

items.learningFocus: General preparedness, no current forecast or unsafe rescue instruction.

tasks.instruction:
Authored practice — not a board or school examination question.
Topic: Preparing for a cyclone warning
Suppose you are Imran and your friend is Sumi. Write a dialogue about family preparedness after an official cyclone warning, emphasising local guidance and adult responsibility.
tasks.answer:
Imran: My family heard an official cyclone warning. How should we prepare?
Sumi: Follow the current instructions from local authorities and discuss the plan with responsible adults.
Imran: We should know the designated shelter and the recommended route before conditions worsen.
Sumi: Yes, and arrange help early for family members who need additional assistance.
Imran: What supplies should the adults consider?
Sumi: They can prepare drinking water, essential documents, a torch and necessary personal supplies according to local advice.
Imran: Should we go near the coast to watch the waves?
Sumi: No. We should avoid exposed places and never ignore an evacuation instruction for photographs.
Imran: We can agree on a contact person in case we are separated.
Sumi: Keep contact details available, but do not publish private information in public groups.
Imran: I will help my family check our plan while it is safe to do so.
Sumi: Good. Preparation means acting early and following reliable instructions, not taking risks.

items.learningFocus: General food literacy, no calorie prescription, weight stigma or individual treatment plan.

tasks.instruction:
Authored practice — not a board or school examination question.
Topic: A varied and affordable diet
Suppose you are Rafi and your friend is Lopa. Write a dialogue about choosing a varied diet within a family budget without judging people’s food choices.
tasks.answer:
Rafi: I often skip lunch and buy a packet of snacks later. I want a more regular routine.
Lopa: Could you discuss an affordable lunch plan with your family?
Rafi: We cannot buy expensive foods every day. Does a varied diet require them?
Lopa: Not necessarily. Local grains, pulses, seasonal vegetables and other available foods can offer variety.
Rafi: I should think about regular meals and drinking water rather than advertisements.
Lopa: Yes, but people have different needs, allergies, beliefs and budgets. We should not judge their plates.
Rafi: Is there one perfect menu for everyone?
Lopa: No. Personal dietary concerns are best discussed with a qualified health professional when possible.
Rafi: I can start by planning tomorrow’s lunch instead of making an unrealistic promise.
Lopa: That sounds practical. Safe food preparation and clean containers matter too.
Rafi: I will avoid wasting food and ask my family which options are manageable.
Lopa: Small, sustainable changes are more useful than copying an expensive online diet.

items.learningFocus: Daily journey planning, distinct from existing road-accident prevention dialogue.

tasks.instruction:
Authored practice — not a board or school examination question.
Topic: Improving a daily bus journey
Suppose you are Adnan and your friend is Joya. Write a dialogue about making a daily public-transport journey more practical and considerate.
tasks.answer:
Adnan: Our families are considering the bus for the journey to school. What should we find out first?
Joya: The route, timetable, fare and safe boarding points, with help from our parents or guardians.
Adnan: We also need to know whether the service is accessible and dependable.
Joya: Exactly. A bus is useful only if it suits the passenger’s needs and the actual route.
Adnan: How can we be considerate when it is crowded?
Joya: Keep the doorway clear, avoid pushing and offer assistance respectfully rather than making assumptions.
Adnan: I will keep my bag close so it does not block another passenger.
Joya: We should also protect our belongings and avoid sharing personal details with strangers.
Adnan: If we miss the bus, we must not run into traffic after it.
Joya: We should use the backup plan agreed with our families instead.
Adnan: Perhaps we can suggest clearer route information to the operator through the school.
Joya: Good idea. Reliable shared transport needs both considerate passengers and responsible service.

items.learningFocus: Renewable-energy evaluation; no installation advice or output/financial guarantees.

tasks.instruction:
Authored practice — not a board or school examination question.
Topic: Considering solar power for school
Suppose you are Arif and your friend is Shila. Write a dialogue about evaluating a proposal for school solar panels, including benefits and practical limits.
tasks.answer:
Arif: The environment club has suggested solar panels for our school. Is it a good idea?
Shila: It may be useful, but the school needs a proper assessment before deciding.
Arif: Sunlight is renewable, so could the panels supply power at every hour?
Shila: No. Output depends on conditions, and electricity at night requires other arrangements.
Arif: We should find out how much electricity the school uses and when it uses it.
Shila: A qualified professional should also assess the site, electrical safety, costs and maintenance.
Arif: Could students climb onto the roof to inspect it?
Shila: No. Site inspection and installation must be left to authorised, trained people.
Arif: We could help by recording classroom electricity use with our teacher’s supervision.
Shila: And reduce unnecessary use of lights and fans where it is appropriate.
Arif: Our proposal should include practical limitations rather than promise free electricity forever.
Shila: Exactly. A responsible recommendation weighs evidence, costs and long-term care.

items.topic: Supporting a classmate facing early marriage
items.learningFocus: Safeguarding without invented helpline/legal ages, public exposure or unsafe confrontation.

tasks.instruction:
Authored practice — not a board or school examination question.
Topic: Supporting a classmate facing early marriage
Suppose you are Rupa and your friend is Ayan. Write a dialogue about obtaining safe, respectful support for a classmate who is worried about an imposed early marriage.
tasks.answer:
Rupa: A classmate told me she is frightened because her family is discussing an early marriage.
Ayan: We should listen without blaming her and ask what support she feels safe accepting.
Rupa: Should we post about her situation online to attract attention?
Ayan: No. That could expose private information and increase the risk to her.
Rupa: A trusted teacher or safeguarding adult may help her find appropriate support.
Ayan: Yes. We should explain our concern privately rather than confront the family ourselves.
Rupa: We must not promise absolute secrecy if her safety is at risk.
Ayan: We can be honest about seeking responsible help while sharing only what is necessary.
Rupa: Her education and wishes matter, and the decision should not be forced on her.
Ayan: A responsible adult can help identify applicable legal and protection services.
Rupa: I will ask our trusted teacher for guidance without spreading the story among classmates.
Ayan: Let us support her choices and safety rather than turn her difficulty into gossip.

items.learningFocus: Pathway comparison distinct from general unemployment/aim-in-life; no institution endorsement.

tasks.instruction:
Authored practice — not a board or school examination question.
Topic: Exploring practical training options
Suppose you are Faisal and your friend is Nitu. Write a dialogue about comparing vocational training options after SSC without assuming one pathway suits everyone.
tasks.answer:
Faisal: I enjoy practical work and want to explore vocational training after SSC.
Nitu: That is worth investigating. Which skills or fields interest you most?
Faisal: I like working with equipment, but I do not know how to compare courses.
Nitu: Check the provider’s recognition, entry requirements, course content, fees and safety arrangements.
Faisal: An advertisement promises that every graduate will immediately get a high-paying job.
Nitu: We should be cautious about guarantees and ask for verifiable information, not just testimonials.
Faisal: I also need to discuss costs and travel with my family.
Nitu: A school adviser may help you compare practical training with other further-study routes.
Faisal: Choosing a practical course should not mean other people regard me as less capable.
Nitu: Of course not. Different pathways require valuable skills and should be considered respectfully.
Faisal: I will visit recognised providers with a trusted adult and prepare questions in advance.
Nitu: An informed choice is better than following either an advertisement or someone else’s prejudice.

items.learningFocus: Evidence-based disagreement, turn-taking and anti-harassment.

tasks.instruction:
Authored practice — not a board or school examination question.
Topic: Respectful debate in class
Suppose you are Saba and your friend is Niloy. Write a dialogue about disagreeing respectfully during a classroom debate.
tasks.answer:
Saba: Our last classroom debate became an argument. How can we avoid that next time?
Niloy: Agree on rules for speaking time, evidence and respectful language before starting.
Saba: Is it acceptable to question another speaker’s evidence?
Niloy: Certainly. We can challenge a claim without insulting the person who makes it.
Saba: Sometimes I interrupt because I am afraid I will forget my point.
Niloy: Write a short note and wait for your turn. The moderator should give everyone a fair chance.
Saba: What if someone admits that a fact they used was wrong?
Niloy: Welcome the correction. Changing a view after checking evidence is not a personal defeat.
Saba: We should also avoid jokes about someone’s accent, identity or background.
Niloy: Yes, and ask the teacher to help if the discussion becomes abusive.
Saba: I will try to summarise the other argument fairly before responding.
Niloy: That will help us understand differences instead of simply trying to speak the loudest.

items.learningFocus: Conservation without invented site history or unsafe amateur restoration.

tasks.instruction:
Authored practice — not a board or school examination question.
Topic: Caring for a heritage building
Suppose you are Riad and your friend is Piya. Write a dialogue about a responsible school visit to a local heritage building.
tasks.answer:
Riad: Our history club plans to visit an old building. How can we make the visit responsible?
Piya: Ask permission, check visitor rules and arrange appropriate adult supervision first.
Riad: We should learn its history from reliable records rather than repeat every local rumour.
Piya: Yes. If an account is uncertain, our report should say so instead of presenting it as fact.
Riad: Some walls look damaged. Could we scrape them clean for a photograph?
Piya: No. Students should not attempt repairs or disturb the fabric of the building.
Riad: We can avoid touching fragile surfaces and stay within the permitted areas.
Piya: Also ask before photographing people and follow any restrictions on photography.
Riad: Perhaps our report could describe why proper conservation needs trained people.
Piya: We could share it with the school and the responsible custodian without disclosing restricted details.
Riad: The visit should leave the site unchanged except for our better understanding.
Piya: Exactly. Appreciating heritage includes respecting the people who care for it.

items.learningFocus: Inquiry and inclusive participation; no hazardous experiment instructions.

tasks.instruction:
Authored practice — not a board or school examination question.
Topic: Starting a school science club
Suppose you are Tanvir and your friend is Esha. Write a dialogue about forming an inclusive school science club with safe, affordable activities.
tasks.answer:
Tanvir: I would like to start a science club, but we have very little money.
Esha: We can begin with teacher-approved observations and discussions rather than expensive equipment.
Tanvir: Could we record plant growth in the school garden?
Esha: Yes, if the school agrees and we use clear measurements without disturbing protected plants.
Tanvir: We should invite students who are curious, not only those with the highest marks.
Esha: Agreed. Members can contribute through drawing, writing, measuring or asking good questions.
Tanvir: What about dramatic experiments we see online?
Esha: We must not copy them without a qualified teacher’s risk assessment and supervision.
Tanvir: We can keep a shared notebook of our methods, results and mistakes.
Esha: And explain that one small observation does not prove a universal claim.
Tanvir: Let us prepare a simple proposal, a meeting plan and an accessible invitation.
Esha: A careful, welcoming club will teach more than an impressive name alone.

items.learningFocus: Habitat/community stewardship; no invented current statistics or risky intervention.

tasks.instruction:
Authored practice — not a board or school examination question.
Topic: Protecting a local wetland
Suppose you are Nabil and your friend is Toma. Write a dialogue about learning how to protect a local wetland while respecting nearby communities.
tasks.answer:
Nabil: Our class wants to help protect the wetland near our village. Where should we begin?
Toma: Learn about its plants, wildlife and the people whose livelihoods depend on it.
Nabil: We should not assume that every local activity causes the same kind of damage.
Toma: Right. Ask our teacher to arrange a respectful discussion with residents and knowledgeable conservation workers.
Nabil: Can we organise a visit to observe birds?
Toma: Only with permission and suitable adult supervision, staying on safe routes and away from nests.
Nabil: We must not catch animals, enter deep water or remove plants for our project.
Toma: We can record observations from a safe distance and avoid disturbing wildlife.
Nabil: What if we see dumping or another serious concern?
Toma: Report it through responsible adults to the relevant authority instead of confronting people ourselves.
Nabil: Our project can explain why habitat protection and community needs must be considered together.
Toma: Yes. Conservation works better through informed cooperation than blame.

items.learningFocus: Non-disturbing school wildlife observation, distinct from wetland land-use/community discussion.

tasks.instruction:
Authored practice — not a board or school examination question.
Topic: Observing wildlife without disturbing it
Suppose you are Mira and your friend is Rashed. Write a dialogue about observing wild birds responsibly around the school grounds.
tasks.answer:
Mira: There is a nest in the tree beside our classroom. Everyone wants to see it closely.
Rashed: We should watch quietly from a distance and avoid crowding the tree.
Mira: Someone suggested moving the nest to a lower branch for better photographs.
Rashed: That could harm the birds. We should not touch or move nests or eggs.
Mira: We can use a teacher-approved observation spot and keep the exact location out of public posts.
Rashed: Good idea. Our notes can describe behaviour without attracting a crowd to the nest.
Mira: Should we bring food to make the birds come closer?
Rashed: Not without appropriate expert guidance. Our aim is to observe, not change their behaviour.
Mira: If we notice an injured bird, we should not chase or handle it ourselves.
Rashed: Tell a responsible adult who can contact an appropriate wildlife professional.
Mira: I will suggest a quiet observation diary instead of a photography competition.
Rashed: That will help us learn while putting the birds’ welfare first.
